articles.title: The Original Billion-Dollar Law Firm
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

Everyone knows Kirkland & Ellis sits atop Biglaw’s money charts today. But before Kirkland, another firm owned the revenue records — pulling off what its own leaders called a “1-2-3 punch” as the first firm ever to cross $1 billion, then $2 billion, then $3 billion in annual revenue, and briefly reigning as the world’s highest-grossing firm before Kirkland knocked it off the top. Name the firm.

Hint: Founded in Los Angeles in 1934, the firm cleared those three milestones in 2003, 2007, and 2017.

See the answer on the next page.

articles.title: The Settlement Mill Is The Part Of Personal Injury Law Nobody Wants To Talk About
articles.content:
There is a term lawyers sometimes use when talking among themselves that you probably won’t find on a law firm’s website.
Settlement mill.
It’s not a particularly flattering description, and that’s the point. It generally refers to a personal injury practice that operates on volume. Bring in as many cases as possible, move them through a relatively standardized process, negotiate settlements, collect fees, and make room for the next group of clients.
Now, I want to be careful here because I think this subject deserves considerably more thought than it usually gets.
Settling personal injury cases is not a bad thing. Quite the opposite. Most cases settle, and many absolutely should. Litigation can be expensive, emotionally exhausting, and painfully slow. A fair settlement can put money into the hands of an injured person when it is needed most, without the uncertainty of asking a jury to decide what happens next.
I’ve recommended settlements throughout my career. I’ve also advised clients against accepting offers that, in my judgment, failed to account for what they had lost.
Both decisions are part of doing the job properly.
My concern is what happens when settling cases becomes less about professional judgment and more about keeping a business operation moving.
And I think we need to talk about that.
When the Business Gets Bigger Than the Case
Personal injury law looks considerably different today than it did when I began practicing.
Advertising is everywhere. Television commercials, billboards, social media campaigns, sponsored search results, and increasingly sophisticated referral networks have turned client acquisition into an enormous industry.
Some firms have become exceptionally good at it. They can generate hundreds or thousands of inquiries, sort through them quickly, sign clients electronically, and move files into systems designed to manage extraordinary volumes of work.
None of that is inherently improper. A large law firm can provide excellent representation. Technology can improve communication, reduce administrative costs, and help lawyers spend more time doing actual legal work.
But attracting cases and representing injured people are two different skills.
The danger comes when a firm becomes so focused on bringing cases through the front door that it builds its entire operation around getting them out the back door just as quickly.
Think about the economics for a moment.
A law firm that resolves 10 cases relatively quickly may collect more in total fees than a firm that spends months developing five difficult cases, even if some of those five eventually produce substantially better results for the clients.
That doesn’t prove anything improper happened. The 10 settlements might all have been perfectly reasonable.
But it illustrates a tension that deserves attention.
The law firm’s business depends on its entire collection of cases. The injured person has only one.
For someone who may never work in the same capacity again, the difference between a $100,000 settlement and a $300,000 settlement isn’t an accounting detail. It might determine whether the mortgage gets paid, whether future treatment is affordable, or whether a family can remain financially secure.
Of course, neither amount means much without knowing the evidence, applicable law, and available insurance. A $100,000 settlement could be an excellent outcome in one case and a deeply inadequate result in another.
That’s precisely why every case needs to be evaluated on its own merits.
The Pressure Nobody Sees
Here’s something many people outside the profession may not appreciate.
A personal injury case often becomes more complicated after the initial investigation, not less.
The police report might establish who caused a crash. Medical records might document a broken leg, a spinal injury, or a traumatic brain injury. Those are important starting points, but they rarely tell the whole story.
What if the injured person was a construction worker who can no longer climb ladders? What if the surgery appeared successful, but chronic pain makes returning to work nearly impossible? What if a physician believes another operation may be necessary several years from now?
A lawyer needs to investigate those questions before confidently advising someone what their claim is worth.
That takes conversations with the client, medical evidence, sometimes expert opinions, and a willingness to investigate facts that aren’t immediately obvious.
And it takes time.
In a high-volume operation, time can become the most carefully rationed resource.
The pressure doesn’t necessarily arrive as an explicit instruction to settle a case cheaply. It can be subtler. A lawyer carries an overwhelming caseload. Staff members are expected to move files toward resolution. Performance is measured through how many cases close and how quickly they close.
Eventually, the path of least resistance can begin to look like the normal way of practicing law.
That’s where I worry about clients getting shortchanged, even when everybody involved believes they’re working hard.
A person can receive a settlement check, thank the law firm, and never realize that important parts of the case weren’t fully explored.
Why the Willingness to Go to Trial Matters
One of the most important things a personal injury lawyer brings to negotiations is the credible possibility of taking the case to court.
I don’t mean threatening trial as a negotiating gimmick. I mean having the experience, preparation, and willingness to follow through when litigation becomes necessary.
Insurance companies evaluate risk. They consider the evidence, potential damages, litigation expenses, and what might happen if a jury hears the case.
The opposing lawyer’s willingness and ability to litigate can be part of that calculation.
A firm that regularly prepares cases for trial may approach negotiations differently from one whose operations depend on resolving nearly everything before meaningful litigation begins.
This doesn’t mean every case should be tried. Some cases have limited available insurance coverage. Others involve serious factual disputes, uncertain medical evidence, or risks that make settlement the sensible choice.
And a trial lawyer who refuses reasonable settlements simply to prove how tough he is isn’t serving clients particularly well either.
What matters is having a genuine choice.
If a lawyer isn’t willing or equipped to pursue litigation when the circumstances warrant it, the client may never have all the options that should be available.
The Questions I’d Ask Before Hiring a Lawyer
People shopping for a personal injury attorney often see advertisements touting enormous verdicts, impressive settlements, and decades of combined experience.
Those results may be meaningful, but they don’t necessarily tell you what will happen after you sign a retainer agreement.
I’d ask who will actually handle my case. Will I have regular access to an attorney? How many active files does that attorney manage? Who makes decisions about settlement strategy? Does the firm litigate cases itself, or does it typically refer them elsewhere when negotiations fail?
I’d also ask what happens if I disagree with a settlement recommendation.
That last question matters because, ultimately, the decision whether to accept a settlement belongs to the client.
A lawyer provides advice, explains risks, and makes recommendations. The client decides whether to settle.
It’s an important distinction, particularly when the injured person feels financial pressure to accept whatever is being offered.
I’d want a lawyer who could explain, in plain English, why an offer makes sense or why it doesn’t. Not simply tell me that it’s the best the insurance company will do.
And I’d want some assurance that the person evaluating my case actually understands my life.
Medical bills are relatively easy to add up. The harder questions concern what someone has lost beyond those bills.
Can a parent still lift a young child? Can someone who worked with their hands for 25 years continue earning a living? What happens to a marriage when chronic pain changes nearly every part of daily life?
Those aren’t details to be plugged into a settlement formula and forgotten.
They’re often the very heart of the case.
We Owe Clients Something Better
I understand why law firms pursue efficiency. There’s a great deal of unnecessary expense and administrative work in litigation. Better technology, better staffing, and better organization can make legal services more accessible and responsive.
But there’s a difference between eliminating unnecessary work and eliminating the work that’s necessary to understand a client’s claim.
Sometimes the right decision is to settle promptly. Sometimes it’s to wait until the long-term medical prognosis becomes clearer. Sometimes it’s to spend money on an expert, pursue another deposition, or file a lawsuit even though doing so makes the case more expensive to handle.
The right answer depends on the client, not the firm’s monthly settlement numbers.
Personal injury lawyers regularly criticize insurers for treating injured people like claim numbers. It’s a fair criticism when the evidence supports it.
But the same standard should apply to us.
I don’t think the solution is to condemn large firms or assume every practice handling a substantial caseload is a settlement mill. That would be unfair to plenty of good lawyers doing difficult work.
I do think we should be more willing to examine the incentives driving our own profession.
Because a settlement isn’t successful merely because a file closes and a check gets issued.
It’s successful when the client makes an informed decision, understands what may be gained or surrendered, and receives representation that reflects the particular facts of that case.
There will always be pressure to grow, generate revenue, and handle more work. Running a law firm is, among other things, running a business.
But the business exists to support the representation. Not the other way around.
The client should never have to wonder whether the recommendation to settle was made because it was genuinely the best available outcome or because another hundred files were waiting to be closed.
That’s a question our profession should be uncomfortable even having to ask.
Michael J. Epstein, a Harvard Law School graduate, is a trial lawyer and managing partner of The Epstein Law Firm, P.A., a law firm based in New Jersey.

articles.title: It’s Always Market Compensation In Philadelphia
articles.content:
How else was I supposed to deal with Dechert? I already used my “Deck the Halls” pun for Choate Hall last night. So we had to dig into the Sunny references.
Dechert informed its team that it will also match the raises and bonuses in light of Cravath’s move. Dechert pulled in something like $1.6 billion in 2025, and profits per equity partner jumped 27 percent. The firm’s been in growth mode all year, starting it off by nabbing more than 20 partners from McDermott and opening offices in Chicago and Dallas, and by late May it was up to 45 lateral partners for the year. It added Randy Mastro in New York and set up Houston around trial lawyer Jim Wetwiska. The firm hired two Weil partners just the other day.
Which is all to say the firm can afford raises. Here’s what it looks like:
Salaries will tick up on January 1 and bonuses will be distributed at the end of January.
I mean… if you have to work with collaborators who’ve spent the last couple years greasing the wheels for frivolous prosecutions of Trump’s political enemies and leading an entity that’s mislead federal judges so often it has lost its long-cherished benefit of the doubt, you might as well get paid!
Congratulations.
